brief.proof: a calculation with its inputs and load case; a simulation with mesh, boundary conditions, material model and a convergence check; a test with specimen count, fixture and instrument; the drawing revision; the standard with its edition and clause.
brief.numbers: always a unit, in one unit system; a dimension with its tolerance; a material with its specification and condition; a safety factor with what it is against (yield, ultimate, fatigue) and the load case; measured, nominal and simulated values told apart.
brief.failures: a part that breaks in test is a result (mode, place, load, cycles). Also report runs that did not converge, a tested part that differs from the drawing, and one specimen read as proof.
brief.never: supplier prices or customer drawings under agreement, export-controlled data, long passages of a paid standard. Never "safe" without the criterion it met.

checks: Does every number carry a unit in one unit system, and every dimension its tolerance, with no silent conversion between systems?
Could another engineer redo each calculation from what is written: inputs, assumptions, method, load case, and each standard with its edition and clause?
Does each simulation state mesh, element type, boundary conditions, contacts and material model, and show a mesh convergence check?
Do the supports, loads and symmetry in a model match how the real part is held and loaded, or do they make it look stiffer or less stressed than it is?
Is each safety factor, margin or claim of safe tied to a named criterion (yield, ultimate, buckling, fatigue), a load case and the source of its allowable?
Does each material carry its specification and condition (temper, heat treatment, orientation), and does each property value come from a cited source?
Does each test give specimen count, fixture, instrument and its calibration, loading rate and environment, and show the scatter between specimens?
Is one specimen or one run read as proof, or is a result stretched beyond the range of loads, temperatures or sizes actually tested?
Does the tested or analyzed part match the cited drawing revision, and are deviations in material, process or dimensions written down?
Are measured, nominal and simulated values labeled apart, and where test and model disagree, is the gap explained rather than tuned away?
Are breaks, runs that did not converge and out-of-tolerance parts reported with mode, place, load and cycles, not dropped or softened?
Does the draft hold supplier prices, customer drawings under agreement, export-controlled data, or long passages of a paid standard?
words: part numbers, assembly and revision nicknames, and the project's own names for load cases, rigs and test series (for example a load case the project calls case C). Not general terms such as yield strength.
